title: Command and Control
summary: Command and Control is the tactic that describes how an adversary maintains communication with compromised systems, tasking them and receiving results through channels that must remain usable while looking as ordinary as possible. Behaviours include beaconing over web protocols to attacker-controlled or compromised sites, tunnelling through DNS, using application layer protocols such as mail or messaging services, abusing legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling and cloud services as relays, and encrypting or encoding traffic to defeat content inspection. From a defender's perspective, this is one of the richest tactics for network and endpoint analytics because sustained communication has structural properties: regularity of timing, consistency of payload size, long-lived sessions to destinations that are new to the environment, and repeated resolution of domains that no user or service should need. Endpoint evidence complements it through process-to-network correlation, showing which binary opened the connection, and through anomalous child processes that inherit a network session. Detection is difficult in isolation because beaconing to a content delivery network resembles software updates, because DNS tunnelling looks like ordinary recursive queries until volume and entropy are considered, and because adversaries deliberately use the same services and protocols as the business. Practical detection combines flow analytics, DNS and proxy logs, TLS metadata such as certificate and JA3-style fingerprints, and endpoint context, plus the discipline to build a baseline of expected egress before hunting for what should not be there.
objectives: Describe the main command and control channels and how each appears in network, DNS, proxy, TLS, and endpoint telemetry.
Analyse beaconing behaviour using interval regularity, jitter, payload size consistency, and destination history rather than content inspection alone.
Detect DNS tunnelling and covert channels by examining query volume, subdomain entropy, and response characteristics.
Correlate endpoint process data with network sessions to attribute an outbound connection to the process that opened it.
Baseline expected egress so that new destinations, unusual protocols, and long-lived sessions stand out.
Explain how egress filtering, protocol allow-listing, and TLS inspection trade off against operational cost and privacy.
